metadata.title: How I build: software engineering standards
metadata.description: Architecture, backend, data, AI, mobile and security: the standards I apply to every project, with this site's measurements as a sample you can verify yourself.

hero.title: Standards you can <highlight>verify</highlight>
hero.description: Claiming to care about quality is easy. This page lists the standards I apply as a software engineer — from the architecture of a backend to an agentic system — and uses this site as the part you can check yourself, right now, without taking my word for it.

scores.title: The verifiable sample
scores.subtitle: Taken with {tool} on {url}, {device} profile, on {date}.
scores.intro: A website is the only part of my work you can audit without my permission: it's public, and standard tools exist to measure it. That's why I use it as a sample. It is not the scope of what I do — it's the part that can be checked.
scores.vitalsHint: Largest Contentful Paint, Cumulative Layout Shift, Time To First Byte. The thresholds considered good are 2.5 s, 0.1 and 800 ms respectively.
scores.reproduce: Open DevTools on any page of this site, Lighthouse tab, mobile profile, and hit Analyze. Nothing in this section asks you to take my word for it.
scores.buildStat: {pages} pages prerendered at build time, generated in {time} ms.
scores.honesty: Lighthouse's Performance category is missing here because its score depends on the network and CPU throttling of the machine running the test: publishing a number without stating those conditions would be misleading. You get the raw metrics instead, which are comparable.

practices.title: The standards, area by area
practices.subtitle: Every line is a design decision, not an intention.

verifiable.title: What you can verify here
verifiable.subtitle: Measurable with public tools, on this domain, in a minute.

underTheHood.title: What a website cannot show
underTheHood.subtitle: The part of the work that lives behind an API, inside an app or in an agentic system — where Lighthouse doesn't reach and design is what counts.

items.1: Skip link to the main content as the first focusable element
items.2: Every control without visible text exposes a translated aria-label
items.3: Accessible name always contains the visible label (WCAG 2.5.3)
items.4: Visible focus on every interactive element, never removed
items.6: ARIA roles only where needed: never override native semantics

items.1: Pages statically prerendered and served from the CDN cache
items.2: Cumulative Layout Shift at zero: no content jumps while loading
items.3: Images in WebP, no asset above 72 KB
items.4: Self-hosted, preloaded fonts, with no third-party requests
items.5: Translations loaded per route: a page never ships catalogs it cannot use
items.6: Server rendering wherever interactivity isn't needed, to avoid paying for hydration

items.1: Canonical URL and hreflang from a single source, with no conflicting signals
items.2: JSON-LD structured data linked into one entity graph with stable @id values
items.3: Multilingual sitemap with alternates declared for every URL
items.4: Public, maintained llms.txt, compliant with the recommendations
items.5: Content present in the served HTML, not produced after hydration
items.6: Permanent 301 redirects from every legacy address, so history isn't lost

items.1: Explicit module boundaries: every unit has a purpose statable in one sentence
items.2: Input validated at the system edge, before any business logic runs
items.3: Typed errors separated by audience: what the user sees versus what the maintainer sees
items.4: Domain state kept separate from transport state, so either can change alone
items.5: Architectural decisions driven by real constraints, not by technology fashion
items.6: Reversible choices when the cost of being wrong is high and the context uncertain

items.1: Schema as the source of truth, with versioned and reversible migrations
items.2: Integrity constraints in the database, not only in application code
items.3: Indexes designed around real queries, not bolted on afterwards to treat symptoms
items.4: N+1 queries treated as design defects, not as load problems
items.5: Caching with explicit invalidation: never a cache whose expiry nobody knows
items.6: PostgreSQL, MongoDB or Redis chosen for the access pattern, not out of habit

items.1: Structured, validated output: no model response enters the system without a schema
items.2: Tool and function calling with explicit contracts and handled failures
items.3: Multi-agent orchestration with declared delegation and responsibilities
items.4: Context treated as a finite resource: what goes in, what gets summarized, what is dropped
items.5: Models interchangeable behind a boundary, local ones via Ollama included
items.6: Cost and latency treated as project requirements, not as end-of-month surprises

items.1: A single React Native and Expo codebase, with no drift between platforms
items.2: Native conventions respected where users expect them
items.3: Offline state designed in, not added once the reports come in
items.4: Automated updates and releases, with traceable versions
items.5: Real products in the stores, not just prototypes: Fast Memo, 1,000+ downloads in 7 languages
items.6: Open-source components extracted and maintained when they outlive the project

items.1: Secrets server-side only: no key ever reachable from the client
items.2: Layered defence on public endpoints: origin, rate limit, CSRF, validation, in that order
items.3: No user input echoed back in error responses
items.4: TypeScript in strict mode, with no exceptions and no weakening of the config
items.5: A CI pipeline that blocks on types, lint and build before every release
items.6: Code that explains itself: explicit names instead of comments, shared constants against divergence

cta.title: Want this level of care on your product?
cta.description: I apply the same standards to client work, from the backend to the mobile app to AI systems. If you need someone who treats quality as a requirement rather than an extra, let's talk.
